title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
authors: Íñigo Zubeldia, Boris Bolliet, Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Pablo Villanueva-Domingo, Miles Cranmer
abstract: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.

infographic.key_insight: Model choice drives AI peer-review error detection most strongly, while verification tools offer gains that depend on the task and scientific domain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate reviewer models before adding scaffolding, then target citation retrieval, computer algebra, and code execution where they provide measurable value.
method: Inject localisable general, mathematical, numerical, and citation errors at three severity levels into real papers.
Measure detection by error type and severity, plus false positives on clean copies.
Test Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer using citation retrieval, computer algebra, and executed code.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 30 astrophysics and ML preprints with 357 injected errors, 12 reviewer systems were evaluated; three frontier models given the same prompt differed by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora.
infographic.watch_item: Tool gains may not generalise across domains: Skepthical’s citation-detection lead in astrophysics was not statistically distinguishable from the best single LLM in ML.
infographic.paper_title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers

title: The Illusion of Diversity: Aligning LLM Exploration via Effective Entropy
authors: Xiaoliang Fu, Jiaye Lin, Yangyi Fang, Cong Qin, Binbin Zheng, Chaowen Hu
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has shifted the alignment paradigm of large language models from subjective preference to objective correctness, yet a fundamental disconnect persists between exploration diversity and reasoning validity. Existing strategies predominantly rely on "blind" entropy metrics, e.g., token-level or global sequence-level entropy, which structurally fail to distinguish between effective reasoning and potential hallucinations. This misalignment creates an illusion of diversity, where high entropy tends to signal chaotic degeneration rather than valuable exploration. To bridge this gap, we introduce Effective Entropy, a validity-aware entropy concept that quantifies diversity exclusively within the valid subspace and systematically filters out the noise of incorrect trajectories. Built on this concept, we instantiate VEPO, a simple Validity-aware Entropy Policy Optimization method that directly incorporates effective entropy into RLVR training. VEPO induces an adaptive attraction dynamic that drives up the probability of under-explored valid trajectories, a mechanism that matches the practical regime of large-scale autoregressive models where sequence probabilities remain extremely small. Experiments on six mathematical reasoning benchmarks with 1.5B and 7B DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models show consistent aggregate accuracy gains over GRPO and competitive repeated-sampling success. A direct evaluation with matched correct counts finds more distinct strategies on commonly solved MATH500 problems, supported by paired statistical tests and three-seed training comparisons.

infographic.key_insight: Effective Entropy measures diversity only among valid reasoning trajectories, separating useful exploration from incorrect-output noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For verifiable math tasks, validity-aware exploration may improve RL training without rewarding diversity that comes from incorrect reasoning.
method: Restrict the entropy measure to the valid trajectory subspace.
Incorporate Effective Entropy into Validity-aware Entropy Policy Optimization (VEPO) for RLVR training.
Increase the probability of under-explored valid trajectories through an adaptive attraction mechanism.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six math benchmarks with 1.5B and 7B DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models, VEPO reports aggregate accuracy gains over GRPO and competitive repeated-sampling success; matched-correct-count MATH500 evaluations find more distinct strategies, supported by paired tests and three-seed comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on reliable validity verification; the abstract does not establish benefits beyond verifiable mathematical reasoning.
infographic.paper_title: The Illusion of Diversity: Aligning LLM Exploration via Effective Entropy

title: Well-Balanced WE-PINNs for the Shallow Water Equations over Smooth and Discontinuous Bathymetries
authors: Ismail Oubarka, Imad Kissami, Mohamed Boubekeur, Imad Elmahi, Fayssal Benkhaldoun
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations without a mesh, but they do not in general preserve the steady states that well-balanced schemes reproduce exactly. We present a well-balanced extension of the weak and entropy PINN (WE-PINN) framework to the shallow water equations over smooth and discontinuous bathymetry. The residual is a weak space--time control-volume identity enforced on randomly placed control volumes that may overlap, so no mesh is needed. In free-surface variables, the geometric source is integrated by parts onto the bed, so that the network is never differentiated, and a cell-local bed-slope correction makes the quadrature reproduce the exact bed increment. Bed discontinuities, located from the bathymetry alone, separate sub-domains carrying independent networks, coupled through conservation of discharge and total head. We prove that the fully discrete residual vanishes identically on the lake at rest for any control-volume family, quadrature order and nominal bed slope, so that the equilibrium is an exact global minimiser of the training objective; that the continuous residual characterises weak solutions; that the slope correction is consistent; and that no approximation with a continuous free surface can satisfy the head condition at a step with non-zero discharge, so that the decomposition is necessary. Numerically, the residual vanishes to round-off on four lake-at-rest configurations over smooth, discontinuous, compound and tabulated beds, and the trained network reaches the equilibrium to round-off under an extended training budget. On seven Riemann problems at a bottom step, covering sub-, super- and critical transitions, the network attains relative $L^1$ free-surface errors between $6.9\times10^{-4}$ and $3.5\times10^{-3}$, and reaches critical states without prescribing them.

infographic.key_insight: A well-balanced WE-PINN formulation exactly preserves lake-at-rest equilibria in its discrete residual, even over discontinuous bathymetry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This mesh-free approach can model shallow-water flow over uneven beds without introducing residual imbalance at still-water equilibria.
method: Enforce weak space–time conservation on randomly placed, potentially overlapping control volumes without differentiating the network.
Integrate the geometric source by parts and correct local bed slopes so quadrature reproduces exact bed increments.
Use independent networks across bed discontinuities, coupled by conservation of discharge and total head.
infographic.evidence_signal: Four lake-at-rest tests achieved round-off residuals; seven bottom-step Riemann problems yielded relative L1 free-surface errors of 6.9×10⁻⁴–3.5×10⁻³ and recovered critical states without prescribing them.
infographic.watch_item: Exact residual balance does not guarantee rapid training convergence: reaching equilibrium to round-off required an extended training budget.
infographic.paper_title: Well-Balanced WE-PINNs for the Shallow Water Equations over Smooth and Discontinuous Bathymetries

title: Entire sig-jump-diffusions, their expected signature and applications to score-based generative modeling
authors: Christa Cuchiero, Francesca Primavera, Sara Svaluto-Ferro
abstract: We develop score-based generative models for time series and standard finite-dimensional data, building on the analytical computation of the expected signature of a new class of jump-diffusions, called entire sig-jump-diffusions. These are semimartingales whose characteristics are given by linear combinations of potentially infinitely many components of their own signature. We show that their expected signature can be computed by solving linear ODEs in the extended tensor algebra, providing a tractable foundation for learning procedures. Specifically, the learning of a generalized score function for jump diffusions, a key ingredient of our generative modeling framework, can be reduced to solving linear ODEs and a deterministic optimization problem. We further prove that polynomial jump-diffusions can be embedded into this framework, and that their expected signature reduces to a finite-dimensional system of linear ODEs. Building on this result, we develop an alternative approach for finite-dimensional data, based on inverse signature matching, a method that learns the score by matching the expected signature of the reverse process with that of the inverse forward signature.

infographic.key_insight: Entire sig-jump-diffusions make expected signatures computable through linear ODEs, enabling score-based generative modeling of time series and finite-dimensional data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework reduces generalized score learning for jump diffusions to linear ODE solves and deterministic optimization.
method: Define jump-diffusions whose characteristics are linear combinations of their own signature components.
Compute expected signatures via linear ODEs; polynomial jump-diffusions admit finite-dimensional systems.
Learn scores directly or, for finite-dimensional data, through inverse signature matching.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical computability and embedding results, but provides no datasets, numerical benchmarks, or empirical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Beyond the polynomial case, implementation may require truncating infinite-dimensional signature systems and controlling approximation error.
infographic.paper_title: Entire sig-jump-diffusions, their expected signature and applications to score-based generative modeling

title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
authors: Wieger Wesselink, Kees Huizing, Huub van de Wetering
abstract: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted verification of scientific algorithms using the Dafny verification system. The workflow integrates algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling, and resource-driven proof optimization. We applied the workflow using Antrhopic's Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 models, combining LLM-driven development with automated testing and verification feedback, while retaining human oversight for correctness-critical decisions and strategic interventions. We evaluate the approach on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. Notably, we verified the Hopfcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, demonstrating that even highly challenging algorithmic verification tasks can be carried out through a structured LLM-assisted workflow. Many of our machine-checked verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development. Our results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows can shift the role of the human verifier from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review, and strategic guidance.

infographic.key_insight: A structured, ten-step LLM-assisted workflow can support complete machine-checked verification of complex algorithms in Dafny while preserving human oversight.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could shift verification effort from detailed proof construction toward specification review, solver diagnosis, and strategic guidance.
method: Formalize algorithms and develop contracts and invariants.
Empirically test invariants and iteratively construct proofs using testing and verification feedback.
Profile verification bottlenecks and optimize proofs under resource constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors evaluated the workflow on 37 graph-theory and labelled-transition-system algorithms, including the Hopcroft–Tarjan triconnectivity test, with many verifications completed within hours to a few days.
infographic.watch_item: Human review remains essential: machine-checked proofs establish compliance with formal specifications, not whether those specifications capture the intended requirements.
infographic.paper_title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny

title: Your Hypergradient is Skewed: Antithetic Neumann Estimation for Bilevel Optimization
authors: Jason Bohne, Pawel Polak, Gary Kazantsev, David Rosenberg
abstract: Bilevel optimization is a core tool in practical machine learning workflows, including hyperparameter tuning, data reweighting, robust learning, reinforcement learning, and imbalanced classification. Hypergradient computation requires the inverse of the inner Hessian, typically estimated via a truncated Neumann series. While existing analyses focus on bias and variance, we show that the product structure of the Neumann series introduces a third source of error: skewness. We identify that, unlike ordinary gradients, whose asymmetry is suppressed by mini-batch averaging, the Neumann estimator amplifies skewness across factors, with the third-moment error growing, under weak contraction, with truncation depth, inner condition number, and per-factor noise asymmetry. This arises in many practical settings such as corrupted labels, outliers, heterogeneous or class-imbalanced datasets. To address this, we introduce the Antithetic Neumann Estimator (ANE), which pairs each Hessian sample with a mirrored counterpart around a reference Hessian and averages the resulting inverse-Hessian estimates. With an exact reference, the antithetic product retains only even-order noise, eliminating all odd-order perturbation terms; with an approximate reference, the residual odd-order contribution is bounded linearly in the reference error. ANE requires only a modification of the Hessian vector step and combines with existing stochastic or variance-reduced bilevel methods. We instantiate ANE-SGD and ANE-VR, the latter adding recursive variance reduction. Across robust regression, data cleaning, offline reinforcement learning, and imbalanced classification, ANE-based methods improve on stochastic and variance-reduced baselines on every task (20 seeds each), lowering loss by 4 to 25% relative to the best baseline; the largest gains, on robust regression, are a 25% lower test loss and a 54% higher test r-squared.

infographic.key_insight: Stochastic Neumann inverse-Hessian estimates can amplify skewness, while antithetic pairing cancels all odd-order noise terms when the reference Hessian is exact.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable hypergradients can improve bilevel learning pipelines affected by corrupted labels, outliers, heterogeneous data, or class imbalance.
method: Pair each sampled Hessian with its mirror around a reference Hessian.
Average paired Neumann inverse-Hessian estimates to cancel odd-order perturbations.
Integrate the modified Hessian-vector step into ANE-SGD or recursively variance-reduced ANE-VR.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four tasks with 20 seeds each, ANE-based methods report 4–25% lower loss than the best baseline, including 25% lower test loss and 54% higher test R² on robust regression.
infographic.watch_item: Exact odd-order cancellation requires an exact reference Hessian; with an approximate reference, residual odd-order contributions are bounded linearly in reference error.
infographic.paper_title: Your Hypergradient is Skewed: Antithetic Neumann Estimation for Bilevel Optimization

title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Non-intrusive Model Reduction under Data Scarcity
authors: Vivian Zhang, Tomoki Koike, Atticus Rex, Elizabeth Qian
abstract: Many-query analyses, in which a computational model is repeatedly evaluated, play an important role in uncertainty quantification and optimization for engineering design. However, many-query analyses can be prohibitively expensive when considering high-fidelity numerical models, especially those governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). Surrogate modeling replaces costly simulations with cheap approximations, enabling practical uncertainty quantification and design workflows. Machine learning (ML) approaches to surrogate modeling have gained significant traction in the development of surrogate models due to their non-intrusive nature; they do not require access to the underlying simulation code. The Operator Inference (OpInf) approach, in particular, fits reduced operators to state and corresponding time derivative data. However, high-fidelity training data is scarce due to limited computational budgets, and OpInf models trained on such scarce data often exhibit high variance, a critical liability in high-risk engineering design. We propose Multifidelity Operator Inference (MF-OpInf), which reduces this variance by supplementing scarce high-fidelity snapshots with abundant low-fidelity data drawn from coarser discretizations of the same problem. MF-OpInf handles data across varying fidelity levels by utilizing a multifidelity linear regression framework to estimate the reduced operators. Numerical experiments on model PDE problems demonstrate that MF-OpInf predicts PDE solution fields with higher accuracy compared to the high-fidelity-only OpInf with the same computational budget.

infographic.key_insight: Multifidelity Operator Inference supplements scarce high-fidelity training data with abundant coarse-model data to reduce variance in learned reduced-order models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate non-intrusive surrogates can make repeated PDE evaluations more affordable for uncertainty quantification and engineering design optimization.
method: Collect scarce high-fidelity snapshots and abundant snapshots from coarser discretizations.
Fit reduced operators from state and time-derivative data using multifidelity linear regression.
Use the learned reduced model for inexpensive solution prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on model PDE problems show more accurate solution-field predictions than high-fidelity-only Operator Inference at the same computational budget.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish how performance changes when coarse discretizations poorly capture high-fidelity dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Non-intrusive Model Reduction under Data Scarcity

title: ControlHarbor: A Benchmark for Control Design by Coding Agents
authors: Jieqiang Wei, Fahad Ali, Jonny Reichwald, Silun Zhang
abstract: LLM agents, i.e., language models run by a harness, can now write, run and debug software autonomously. This raises the question of whether they can also carry out control system design. In this paper, we consider control system design as a task for LLM agents and grade the designed controller as control engineers do: the controller is given in a single Python file mapping measurements to actions, evaluated on held-out seeds against an ordered set of requirements, under specified physical perturbations and structural certificates, without using neural networks. We formulate the task as a chance-constrained feasibility problem and instantiate it in ControlHarbor, a benchmark of 44 tasks over 13 plants, which includes network consensus, vehicle platooning, the MuJoCo hopper, walker and humanoid. The tasks are packaged in the Harbor format, so that any agent harness can be run against them, and the same environments also serve learning algorithms other than LLMs, such as reinforcement learning (RL), under the same evaluation. With ControlHarbor, we observe that the controllers designed by three frontier coding agents, Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5, reach the RL return on every parity task, but only in a minority of sessions. We also observe that the controllers certified for return alone usually fail under perturbations. When robustness is part of the specification, a structured design meets it at the RL return on the humanoid task, where domain-randomised RL does not; under large pushes, domain-randomised RL succeeds and no designed controller does. The benchmark, the controllers, and their grades are released.

infographic.key_insight: Coding agents can design non-neural controllers that match reinforcement-learning returns, but success is inconsistent and return alone does not establish robustness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: ControlHarbor evaluates executable controllers against ordered requirements, physical perturbations and structural certificates, helping distinguish high performance from specification compliance.
method: Formulate controller design as a chance-constrained feasibility problem.
Submit a single Python file mapping measurements to actions, without neural networks.
Evaluate on held-out seeds using Harbor-packaged tasks shared with learning algorithms.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 44 tasks over 13 plants, three frontier coding agents reached RL returns on every parity task, but only in a minority of sessions.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness remains conditional: a structured design met the humanoid robustness specification at RL return, but no designed controller succeeded under large pushes where domain-randomised RL did.
infographic.paper_title: ControlHarbor: A Benchmark for Control Design by Coding Agents

title: Optimal higher order convergence rates for the MUON optimizer
authors: Thomas Beretti, Thang Do, Steffen Dereich, Arnulf Jentzen
abstract: Gradient descent optimization methods are the key tools to train deep neural networks in artificial intelligence systems. In practice, one typically employs suitable accelerated gradient descent optimization methods such as the momentum optimizer, the Adam optimizer, or the MUON optimizer proposed by Jordan et al. in 2024. In 1964 Polyak showed that, in a neighborhood of a local minimizer, the momentum optimizer converges with the rate $(\sqrtχ+1)^{-1}(\sqrtχ-1)$, which is strictly faster than the rate $(χ+1)^{-1}(χ-1)$ of the standard gradient descent optimizer, where $χ\in(1,\infty)$ is the condition number (the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue) of the Hessian of the objective function at the local minimizer. Recently, the same faster rate has been established for the Adam optimizer. In this work we show that the MUON optimizer achieves the same higher speed of convergence and we establish the optimality of the obtained convergence rates. More specifically, we propose a precise concept for measuring the speed of convergence of gradient descent optimization methods, and we establish optimal convergence rates for the standard gradient descent, the momentum, the RMSprop, the Adam, and the MUON optimizers.

infographic.key_insight: MUON achieves the optimal local convergence rate (√χ−1)/(√χ+1), matching momentum and Adam and improving on standard gradient descent’s rate (χ−1)/(χ+1), where χ is the local Hessian condition number.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result gives theoretical support for MUON’s accelerated convergence near a local minimizer, rather than guaranteeing faster end-to-end neural network training.
method: Define a precise measure of optimizer convergence speed.
Establish optimal rates for gradient descent, momentum, RMSprop, Adam, and MUON.
Relate local convergence rates to Hessian conditioning.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence and optimality results, but no datasets, empirical benchmarks, or runtime measurements.
infographic.watch_item: The highlighted rates are local; the abstract does not specify the tuning requirements or assumptions needed to attain them in practical training.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal higher order convergence rates for the MUON optimizer

title: Learning Rate Transfer and Feature Learning Across Depth for Constrained Spectral Optimizers: Complete Scion
authors: Eline Pot, Laurent Lefebvre, Mathieu Segond, Antonio Silveti-Falls
abstract: Hyperparameter transfer across model depth is instrumental in training deep models, as it enables learning rates calibrated on shallow networks to be effectively applied to deeper architectures. The recent CompleteP framework establishes a $1/L$ residual scaling rule that demonstrates this for Adam-family optimizers. We study whether similar transfer extends to constrained optimization methods, specifically Frank-Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent, where updates are determined by linear minimization oracles. We derive scaling rules for these methods which confirm that the $1/L$ residual scaling applies, although the arguments differ from the Adam-family optimizers. Our analysis supports depth-wise transfer and width-wise transfer of the learning rate for the Scion algorithm while ensuring feature learning and avoiding the kernel-regime. In experiments on NLP transformers (nanoGPT on FineWeb), vision transformers (DeiT on ImageNet), and vision MLPs (MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10), we observe learning rate transfer across depth and feature learning for appropriately chosen residual scaling.

infographic.key_insight: A 1/L residual scaling rule supports learning-rate transfer across depth for constrained spectral optimizers while preserving feature learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For Scion, the derived scaling rules support reusing learning rates across model depth and width, potentially reducing hyperparameter tuning.
method: Analyze Frank–Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent with linear minimization oracles.
Derive depth-scaling rules that recover 1/L residual scaling through arguments distinct from Adam-family analyses.
Establish conditions supporting feature learning rather than kernel-regime behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments report depth-wise learning-rate transfer and feature learning in nanoGPT on FineWeb, DeiT on ImageNet, and MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10 with appropriate residual scaling.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer depends on appropriate residual scaling; the abstract does not quantify tuning savings or establish universality across architectures.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Rate Transfer and Feature Learning Across Depth for Constrained Spectral Optimizers: Complete Scion

title: Fit-LRP: Fitting Linear Relaxations to Polytopes for Neural Network Verification over Non-Convex Regions
authors: Brian Yarbrough, Jesse Wayment, Jingbo Wang, Philip E. Paré, Shreyas Sundaram
abstract: State-of-the-art neural network verifiers evaluate linear relaxations over axis-aligned bounding boxes. However, verification domains in cyber-physical systems are rarely boxes. Reachability specifications, obstacle-avoidance constraints, and neural Lyapunov certificates typically yield oblique or non-convex polyhedral regions, over which box-based bounds become extremely loose. This paper proposes Fit-LRP (Fitting Linear Relaxations to Polytopes), a framework the implements exact optimization of affine bounds over non-convex domains (represented by unions of polytopes) by solving a sequence of small, low-dimensional linear programs. Our approach seamlessly enhances the final optimization step of LiRPA and $α,\! β$-CROWN branch-and-bound (BaB) algorithms. In BaB verification, approximating oblique constraints with axis-aligned splits causes severe combinatorial blowup and risks non-termination. By optimizing the final affine bound of a nonlinear function over the exact polyhedral state-space constraints our method eliminates box-induced over-approximations, enabling earlier search-tree pruning. On ARCH-COMP and neural Lyapunov benchmarks, Fit-LRP reduces branching on the hardest region by $47\times$, cuts worst-case verification time by $15\times$, and with region-wise partitioning, verifies on a single CPU $6.1\times$ faster than $α,\! β$-CROWN on a GPU.

infographic.key_insight: Fit-LRP tightens neural network verification bounds by optimizing affine relaxations over exact unions of polytopes rather than loose axis-aligned bounding boxes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It supports verification over oblique and non-convex regions arising in reachability, obstacle avoidance, and neural Lyapunov certification.
method: Represent non-convex verification domains as unions of polytopes.
Optimize affine bounds over these domains using small, low-dimensional linear programs.
Integrate with the final bound-optimization step of LiRPA and α,β-CROWN branch-and-bound to enable earlier pruning.
infographic.evidence_signal: On ARCH-COMP and neural Lyapunov benchmarks, the abstract reports 47× less branching on the hardest region, 15× lower worst-case verification time, and—with region-wise partitioning—6.1× faster verification on one CPU than α,β-CROWN on a GPU.
infographic.watch_item: Exact domain optimization does not make the neural network relaxation exact; scalability may depend on domain dimension and the number of polytopes.
infographic.paper_title: Fit-LRP: Fitting Linear Relaxations to Polytopes for Neural Network Verification over Non-Convex Regions

title: Riordan Arrays as Structured Operators for Artificial Intelligence
authors: Dennis Davenport, Dewayne A. Dixon, Moussa Doumbia
abstract: Riordan arrays have traditionally been studied as infinite lower-triangular matrices that encode generating-function transformations and combinatorial relationships. This note proposes a complementary direction: using Riordan arrays as structured operators in artificial intelligence and data analysis. For a data sequence with generating function $A(z)$, a Riordan array $(g(z),f(z))$ produces the transformation \[ A(z)\longmapsto g(z)A(f(z)). \] This yields a parameterized family of causal linear operators that combine convolution, substitution, and multiscale mixing. The resulting structure may support parameter-efficient neural-network layers, variable-length sequence models, interpretable recurrent systems, invertible architectures, and models for hierarchical or recursively generated data. We explain what the infinite-dimensional viewpoint does and does not provide, outline several possible architectures, identify theoretical and numerical challenges, and propose an initial experimental program. The aim is not to claim that Riordan arrays are appropriate for all data, but to identify settings in which their algebraic structure supplies a useful inductive bias.

infographic.key_insight: Riordan arrays could provide an algebraically structured inductive bias for AI through causal linear transformations A(z) → g(z)A(f(z)).
infographic.engineering_relevance: The structure may enable parameter-efficient sequence layers, interpretable recurrent systems, and invertible architectures for hierarchical data.
method: Represent a data sequence by its generating function A(z).
Apply a Riordan operator (g(z), f(z)) to combine convolution, substitution, and multiscale mixing.
Explore neural architectures based on these structured operators.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract outlines possible architectures and an initial experimental program, but reports no datasets, benchmarks, or measured results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical implementations must address finite truncation and numerical stability; the infinite-dimensional formulation alone does not establish effectiveness.
infographic.paper_title: Riordan Arrays as Structured Operators for Artificial Intelligence

title: Does a Self-Learning Migration Agent Learn? An Audited Evaluation of Evidence-Graded Experience Memory for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL Migration
authors: Oleg Grynets, Vasyl Lyashkevych, Valeriia Oliferuk, Vladyslav Babenko, Danylo Kovalchuk, Dmytro Kostetskyi
abstract: Do large language model (LLM) migration agents learn from accumulated experience, or do apparent gains reflect retrieval and reference reuse? We evaluate an evidence-graded agent for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration across four studies. On 1,833 documentation-derived source-reference pairs, persistent memory improved reference conformity (RC) over a no-memory baseline by 0.015 [0.004, 0.025], while policy adaptation added no gain (-0.004 [-0.010, 0.001]). An audit found that 264 of 367 held-out units (72%) shared a PostgreSQL reference with training, and the memory effect on the 103 leak-free units fell to 0.002 [-0.008, 0.011]. A model-free nearest-target copy baseline scored RC 0.222, outperforming all LLM systems (at most 0.163). A reference-grouped split reduced copying to 0.119; a rerun on 374 units in 118 independent target groups found no statistically distinguishable memory effect (0.005 [-0.003, 0.017]) and no policy effect. A separate Oracle-grounded evaluation on 216-224 real PL/SQL units showed that 10-22% of PostgreSQL-accepted units were behaviorally incorrect; a human-gated fix cycle increased demonstrably correct units from 98/216 to 167/224. A write-back study showed a 54% decline in retrieval margin as the knowledge base grew from 12 to 1,200 entries. We derive six evaluation rules that distinguish cross-task learning from reference leakage, copying, metric artifacts, and unstable feedback.

infographic.key_insight: Apparent learning gains in an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration agent largely disappeared after controlling for shared references, with no clear benefit from policy adaptation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate migration agents with reference-disjoint tests and behavioral checks, because retrieval success and PostgreSQL acceptance do not establish correct migration.
method: Compared persistent memory and policy adaptation against no-memory and nearest-target copy baselines.
Audited reference overlap and reran evaluation with reference-grouped splits.
Tested real PL/SQL behavior, human-gated fixes, and retrieval stability as memory grew.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four studies, 72% of the initial held-out units shared training references; on 103 leak-free units, the memory effect on reference conformity was 0.002 with an interval spanning zero [-0.008, 0.011].
infographic.watch_item: PostgreSQL acceptance is not semantic correctness: 10–22% of accepted units in the Oracle-grounded evaluation were behaviorally incorrect.
infographic.paper_title: Does a Self-Learning Migration Agent Learn? An Audited Evaluation of Evidence-Graded Experience Memory for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL Migration

title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
authors: Hans-Martin Will
abstract: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of the same claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks strong normalization and renders algorithmic conversion non-transitive. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed propositional axiom ($irrel : ΠP{:}Prop.\,Πp,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant $Π$-subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction and are sound and complete for declarative typing. Third, we organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with explicit axiom policies (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance semiring support $supp(j,P)$, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records (TTR) to type open-world knowledge graphs. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.

infographic.key_insight: Eigenius separates computational equality from propositional proof irrelevance so verified scientific knowledge can retain distinct derivations and their provenance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Preserving derivation provenance can support evidence comparison and dependency-aware retraction when assays, reagents, or models are invalidated.
method: Define a dependent type kernel with rewrite-based equality and explicitly witnessed proof irrelevance.
Unify universe, function, and ontology subtyping through coercion-free subsumption.
Integrate external verifiers, explicit axiom policies, provenance tracking, and record-typed open-world knowledge graphs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistency, subject reduction, typing soundness and completeness, and Lean 4 mechanization with zero sorry axioms, but no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability and practical integration with scientific data pipelines and external verifiers remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science

title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory
authors: Anif N. Shikder, Ramit Dey, Jan Minac, Lyle E. Muller
abstract: State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order. We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow. Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers. This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.

infographic.key_insight: Commuting diagonal transitions limit SSMs to tracking commutative groups; quaternion channels enable order-sensitive group tracking.
infographic.engineering_relevance: HyperSSM preserves linear-time inference and parallel training while enabling compact, interpretable memory for structured sequential tasks.
method: Model sequence updates as a linear representation of the input-sequence monoid.
Characterize group tracking through transition-group quotients and real, complex, and quaternion blocks.
Add quaternion channels in HyperSSM to represent noncommuting transitions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports exact benchmark group-task solutions using at most five state numbers, including S5 with 32 generators, and generalization to sequences 25× longer than training sequences.
infographic.watch_item: The reported successes concern structured group-tracking tasks; broader language-modeling benefits remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory

title: Weighted STSAFT-Modulation Spaces and Approximation by Phase-Adapted Neural Networks
authors: Ming Hu, Bei Liu, Bolin Liu, Jie Shen
abstract: We develop a transform-adapted approximation framework for shallow neural networks based on the short-time special affine Fourier transform (STSAFT). Replacing the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) in the definition of classical modulation spaces, we work with weighted STSAFT-modulation spaces, building on the existing SAFT-associated modulation-space framework, and use their chirp correspondence with classical weighted modulation spaces through the chirp factorization of the SAFT kernel. We construct an associated neural dictionary and establish an $N$-term Sobolev approximation bound of order $N^{-1/2}$ on bounded one-dimensional domains. A global approximation theorem is also obtained when the spatial translation parameter ranges over the whole real line; a compact-support argument explains why an unrestricted global conclusion cannot in general be inferred from a bounded translation range. For a fixed-scale chirp family $f_κ(x)=e^{iπκx^2}u(x)$, we combine the global estimate with a phase analysis to obtain the stronger phase-dependent upper-bound factor $\langleλ\rangle^n\langleκ-λ\rangle^{n+3/2-1/r}.$ For each fixed nonzero Schwartz envelope, matching the dictionary phase reduces the growth of this specified upper bound from order $|κ|^{n+3/2-1/r}$ to order $|κ|^n$, while preserving the $N^{-1/2}$ rate. The associated mismatch scale is stated as a comparison of upper bounds, not as a threshold for the optimal approximation error. Four numerical experiments examine model comparison, error decay with dictionary size, phase mismatch, and the obstruction caused by restricted translations. We discuss the effective number of fitted output coefficients, including the rank loss of the sine branch at zero phase, and distinguish the numerical diagnostics from the theoretical best-approximation estimates.

infographic.key_insight: Phase-adapted shallow neural dictionaries achieve N^(-1/2) Sobolev approximation bounds, while matching a chirped target’s phase reduces the phase-dependent growth of the stated upper bound.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Encoding known oscillatory phase into neural features offers a principled approach to approximating chirped signals without changing the guaranteed N^(-1/2) rate.
method: Define weighted STSAFT-modulation spaces and connect them to classical modulation spaces through chirp factorization.
Construct a transform-adapted neural dictionary and prove bounded-domain and global N-term approximation estimates.
Analyze phase matching for fixed-scale chirp families to sharpen the phase-dependent upper bound.
infographic.evidence_signal: Four numerical experiments examine model comparison, dictionary-size error decay, phase mismatch, and the obstruction caused by restricted translations.
infographic.watch_item: Global guarantees require unrestricted translations; phase-mismatch comparisons concern upper bounds, not thresholds for optimal approximation error.
infographic.paper_title: Weighted STSAFT-Modulation Spaces and Approximation by Phase-Adapted Neural Networks

title: Agentic Computational Algebra
authors: Ryan A. Anderson, Matthew Trager, Ben Bowman, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
abstract: We explore the use of AI agents for solving computational problems in algebra. For the problems we consider, the main challenge is not correctness but \emph{time}: general-purpose algorithms are guaranteed to provide correct solutions but can be prohibitively slow, while reformulations that exploit special structure often allow solving a problem much faster. We propose to use this setting to evaluate how effectively agents discover and exploit structure within and across tasks to reduce computational costs. More broadly, computational algebra supplies infinitely many problems with independently verifiable answers and systematically controllable structure and difficulty. To illustrate these possibilities, we use benchmark families of systems with controlled shared structure and evaluate agents in three settings: solving independent instances, solving online streams of related instances using persistent memory, and compiling a fast reusable solver for a known problem family. Our experiments show that (i) agents can extend the range of systems solvable within a fixed budget, although reasoning overhead can sometimes outweigh computational savings; (ii) memory can reduce the cost of repeated solving but may preserve suboptimal strategies; (iii) compilation produces faster reusable solvers but at substantial upfront cost. Overall, computational algebra offers concrete, measurable targets for improving how agents discover and reuse structure.

infographic.key_insight: AI agents can accelerate computational algebra by discovering and reusing problem structure, but their reasoning costs can offset the savings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structured algebra benchmarks offer verifiable tests of whether agent-driven optimization reduces total computational cost.
method: Construct system families with controlled shared structure and difficulty.
Evaluate independent solving and online solving with persistent memory.
Compile reusable solvers for known problem families.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments show agents solve more systems within fixed budgets, memory can reduce repeated-solving costs, and compilation yields faster reusable solvers at substantial upfront cost.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluate end-to-end cost: reasoning and compilation overhead can erase gains, while memory may retain suboptimal strategies.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Computational Algebra

title: Sharp Covering-Number Bounds for Feedforward ReLU Networks via Parameter Symmetries
authors: Ruizhi Deng, Guohao Shen, Tangrui Xiong
abstract: In neural networks, distinct parameter configurations often realize the same input--output mapping, indicating that nominal parameter counts can overstate functional complexity. In this paper, we characterize the parameter-space symmetries of ReLU and Leaky ReLU networks across fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures. We prove that every quasianalytic parameter map preserving the network function is a composition of positive channel scaling and channel permutation. By quotienting out both symmetries, we derive uniform covering-number upper bounds in which positive scaling reduces the complexity exponent from the total parameter count $S$ to $S-H$ (with $H$ denoting the number of scalable channels) and permutation symmetry divides the bound by the factorial count $G$ of channel permutations. We establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponent $S-H$ is sharp in general and that the divisor $G$ is attained for one-hidden-layer and generically identifiable networks. We further extend these results to general continuous piecewise-linear activated networks. Finally, we apply our covering-number bounds to derive statistical risk guarantees for empirical risk minimization and capacity control beyond i.i.d.\ settings, and show how the underlying symmetries help explain weight rebalancing in function approximation and flat directions in empirical risk optimization.

infographic.key_insight: Quotienting out function-preserving channel scaling and permutations yields covering-number bounds with a sharp exponent S−H rather than S and a factorial divisor G.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Symmetry-aware capacity measures can sharpen statistical risk guarantees and help explain weight rebalancing and flat optimization directions.
method: Characterize quasianalytic function-preserving parameter maps as compositions of positive channel scaling and permutation.
Derive symmetry-reduced covering bounds for fully connected, convolutional, and residual ReLU/Leaky ReLU networks.
Prove matching lower bounds and extend the analysis to general continuous piecewise-linear activations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical proofs rather than empirical benchmarks: the exponent S−H is sharp in general, while the divisor G is attained for one-hidden-layer and generically identifiable networks.
infographic.watch_item: The symmetry characterization assumes quasianalytic parameter maps, and tightness of the permutation divisor is established only for specified network classes.
infographic.paper_title: Sharp Covering-Number Bounds for Feedforward ReLU Networks via Parameter Symmetries

title: Proximal point algorithm for interval valued optimization problems with application to lasso problem
authors: Anurag Jayswal, Sunidhi, Caihong Han
abstract: In this paper, we consider a class of unconstrained interval valued optimization problems and using a suitable scalarization technique, we formulate an associated scalarized optimization problem and establish the relationships between the optimal solution of the scalarized problem and the $LU$-nondominated solution of the considered optimization problem. Based on this framework, we propose a proximal point algorithm and derive the global convergence of the sequence generated by the proposed algorithm along with the sublinear and linear rate of convergence for convex and strongly convex cases, respectively. Finally, we provide suitable numerical experiments along with comparative analysis with an existing method and applicability of the proposed algorithm on an interval valued lasso regression problem, highlighting its potential in machine learning models with uncertain data.

infographic.key_insight: Scalarization connects interval-valued optimization to scalar problems, enabling a proximal point algorithm with global convergence and sublinear or linear rates under convexity or strong convexity, respectively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a principled approach to interval-valued lasso regression for machine learning with uncertain data.
method: Formulate an associated scalar optimization problem using scalarization.
Establish relationships between scalar optima and interval-valued LU-nondominated solutions.
Develop a proximal point algorithm and analyze convergence rates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments, comparison with an existing method, and an interval-valued lasso application, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Convergence rates depend on convexity assumptions; practical cost and sensitivity to scalarization choices are not detailed in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Proximal point algorithm for interval valued optimization problems with application to lasso problem

title: A Convex-Analytic Reformulation for Poisoning Attacks on Logistic Regression
authors: Carina Moreira Costa, Maria Eduarda Pinheiro, Martin Schmidt
abstract: We study data poisoning attacks on logistic regression with $\ell_2$-regularization, where an attacker chooses the features of a fixed number of injected observations with prescribed labels to maximize the logistic loss on the clean training data. Strong convexity of the defender's problem yields an exact reformulation through its first-order optimality conditions. Using convex conjugacy of the softplus function, we replace the sigmoid relations by a single convex optimality-gap inequality and express the attacker's objective as a concave function. A change of variables makes the stationarity condition affine, leaving bounded bilinear equalities as the only nonconvex constraints. We derive finite bounds on all variables involved in these equalities, including a global bound on the coefficient norm and tighter bounds obtained by preprocessing based on convex optimization. Experiments on eight binary classification datasets evaluate attack effectiveness and compare the two reformulations when solved with \textsf{SCIP}. Attacks obtained by local optimization degrade predictive performance on most datasets, while the convex-analytic formulation produces substantially stronger reported dual bounds within a fixed time limit.

infographic.key_insight: Convex conjugacy yields an exact reformulation of logistic-regression poisoning attacks in which bounded bilinear equalities are the only nonconvex constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The reformulation supports solver-based analysis of poisoning vulnerability in ℓ₂-regularized logistic regression, with stronger reported dual bounds under a fixed compute budget.
method: Replace the strongly convex defender problem with its first-order optimality conditions.
Use softplus conjugacy to encode sigmoid relations through one convex optimality-gap inequality and express the attack objective as concave.
Transform stationarity into affine constraints and bound bilinear variables using global estimates and convex preprocessing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on eight binary classification datasets found that locally optimized attacks degraded predictive performance on most datasets, while the convex-analytic formulation gave substantially stronger reported dual bounds in SCIP.
infographic.watch_item: Bilinear equalities remain nonconvex, so an exact reformulation does not guarantee a globally optimal attack within the time limit.
infographic.paper_title: A Convex-Analytic Reformulation for Poisoning Attacks on Logistic Regression
